strengths: PST addresses a useful evaluation gap: gender stereotyping when textual prompts describe two people together. This is relevant to multimodal NLP, and the organizational-power setting extends the analysis beyond occupation alone.

The occupational experiment systematically covers 800 ordered combinations of 20 male-stereotyped and 20 female-stereotyped occupations, including both left/right orders. The reported paired-generation results provide substantial descriptive evidence of stereotype adherence.

Three human annotators per image and Fleiss’ kappa values of 0.88–0.92 support annotation consistency. Checking BLIP against human judgments and avoiding its unreliable paired-image classifications is appropriate.
The prompt templates, descriptor lists, annotation instructions, and detailed results in the appendices make the evaluation design understandable and support partial reproducibility.
weaknesses: The central interpretation conflates directional stereotype adherence with fairness. SS averages signed values, so opposing imbalances cancel: Table 2 combines female SS = 50 and male SS = −30 into an overall score of 10. A generator depicting only women would score zero across equally weighted male- and female-stereotyped occupations, despite violating the paper’s stated parity criterion. Thus, low single-person SS does not establish fairness, and higher paired SS does not by itself establish greater overall gender imbalance. Report directional stereotyping separately from deviations from parity within each occupation or role.

The headline percentage of biased images is insufficiently calibrated. Figure 4’s PST(Any) counts an image whenever either person follows a stereotype; independent, gender-balanced assignments would satisfy this criterion 75% of the time. Comparing the reported 74.3% with 55% for single-person images therefore does not establish amplification. The marginal scores and PST(Both) provide stronger evidence. The numbers also need reconciliation: with the same fully classified image set, SS in percentage points equals Both% + Any% − 100, implying 46.2 for occupations rather than Table 2’s 47.38.

Statistical support is inadequate for the occupation-specific reversals and amplification claims. The single-person baseline has only three images per identity, while occupational PST has one generation per ordered prompt. Three observations cannot reliably establish that an occupation is anti-stereotypical, especially when highlighting the largest observed changes. The organizational-power experiment samples only a subset of role combinations. More baseline samples, explicit matching of sampled roles across conditions, and uncertainty estimates accounting for shared occupations and paired subjects are needed.

The evaluation does not establish whether depicted occupations and organizational roles actually match the requested left/right assignments. Annotators judge gender traits using the supplied role and position; high agreement on appearance does not validate role binding or compliance with the two-person instruction. Report generation failures, role-assignment accuracy, disagreement resolution, and how the available 'Cannot Identify' responses enter score denominators.

The mitigation conclusions exceed the evidence. One intervention template, evaluated on selected highly biased occupations, cannot establish that prompt-based mitigation generally fails. For organizational power, SS changes from 18.98 to −11.12, reducing the absolute aggregate score while changing direction. Establishing problematic overcorrection requires uncertainty estimates, disaggregated outcomes, and a clearly defined fairness objective.

Reproducibility and claim scope need tightening. The manuscript omits the DALL-E-3 access interface, generation dates, relevant settings, and whether effective prompts were automatically rewritten. Exact sampled role combinations and raw annotations are unavailable, with release promised only after acceptance. Section 3.2.2 also states 944 prompts despite the stated components totaling 1,952. A single-model case study can be valuable, but broader claims about T2I systems require qualification. The measurement and validation gaps warrant revision before a sound Findings recommendation.
